title: Time Zones Will Ruin Your Day
description: Dates the way production hits them. Local times that never happen, offsets that are not time zones, instants versus wall clocks, leap seconds, ISO 8601 traps, meetings that drift across a DST boundary, and why `new Date("2026-01-15")` is not the day you meant. Every answer is checked against a spec, a database, or a runnable snippet.

questions.title: What does `getDate()` return here on a server running in `America/New_York`?

options.text: `0`, because `getDate()` is zero-based like `getMonth()`
`NaN`, because the string has no time component

questions.explanation:
ECMAScript reads the bare `YYYY-MM-DD` form as UTC. The instant is therefore `2026-01-15T00:00:00.000Z`, which in New York (UTC-5 in January) falls on January 14 at 19:00. `getDate()` reports the local day, so you get `14`.

```bash
TZ=America/New_York node -e 'console.log(new Date("2026-01-15").getDate())'
# 14
```

This is probably the most common date bug in web apps. A date picker sends `"2026-01-15"`, the server turns it into an instant, and every user west of Greenwich sees the day before.

The fix is to stop routing calendar dates through instants at all. Keep the value in a type that has no time and no zone, such as `Temporal.PlainDate`, `java.time.LocalDate`, or a Postgres `date` column. If you are stuck with `Date`, at least read it back with `getUTCDate()` so the two ends agree.

questions.title: Why do `new Date("2026-01-15")` and `new Date("2026-01-15T00:00:00")` produce different instants?
questions.description: Both run in `America/New_York`. The first yields `2026-01-15T00:00:00.000Z`; the second yields `2026-01-15T05:00:00.000Z`.

options.text: The spec treats date-only forms as UTC but date-time forms with no offset as local time
The second string is invalid ISO 8601, so the engine falls back to implementation-defined parsing
Both are UTC; the difference comes from the engine applying a DST correction
The first is UTC only when the day is in winter; in summer both are local

questions.explanation:
The asymmetry is written into the language. Where the UTC offset is missing, the spec says date-only forms mean UTC and date-time forms mean local time. Typing `T00:00:00`, which looks like it adds nothing, quietly moves the instant by your entire offset.

That is a deliberate decision rather than a bug, and it is the reason linters flag `new Date(string)` at all. Include an explicit `Z` or `+05:30` whenever you mean a specific instant.

questions.title: What integer does `new Date("2026-01-15T12:00:00Z").getTimezoneOffset()` return with `TZ=America/New_York`?
questions.description: Answer with the number only, including a minus sign if the result is negative.
questions.explanation:
`300`. New York is UTC-5 in January, but the method returns UTC minus local time in minutes, so zones behind UTC come back positive. The sign is inverted compared to the `-05:00` you would write in a timestamp.

```bash
TZ=America/New_York node -e 'const d=new Date("2026-01-15T12:00:00Z"); console.log(d.getTimezoneOffset())'
# 300
```

Call it again in July and you get `240`, because the offset is now UTC-4. One number describes an instant in a zone, never the zone by itself.

Getting the sign backwards is how `+` and `-` end up swapped in hand-rolled offset formatters.

questions.title: What time zone does a JavaScript `Date` instance store internally?

images.alt: Three stacked layers. An instant is milliseconds since the epoch — one absolute point, with no zone and no calendar. An offset such as −04:00 is a number that was true at one instant and names no rules, since dozens of places share it every July. An IANA zone such as America/New_York is a rulebook saying which offset applies when, past and future, rewritten whenever a government changes the law. Beside them, what to store: a log line or past event as a UTC instant; a meeting at 09:00 next year as wall time plus an IANA zone, because the rules may change first; a date of birth as a plain calendar date; a weekly recurring event as wall time plus a zone, which is what iCalendar does. A closing list covers a JS Date holding one number and no zone, EST being a fixed −05:00 while the zone switches, Etc/GMT+5 actually meaning UTC−05:00, an offset never naming a zone, and a 2023 meeting stored as a UTC instant firing an hour late once Mexico dropped DST.
images.caption: The instant stayed correct; the intention — nine in the morning, where they live — did not.

options.text: None. It holds only a count of milliseconds since the Unix epoch
The zone that was active when the object was constructed
UTC, plus the offset it was parsed with
The zone named in the string it was parsed from, defaulting to the host zone

questions.explanation:
A `Date` is one number: `[[DateValue]]`, milliseconds since `1970-01-01T00:00:00Z`. No zone field, no memory of how it was built.

The zone comes in at call time, from the accessor you pick. `getHours()` uses the host zone, `getUTCHours()` uses UTC, `toString()` renders in the host zone. That is why the same object prints differently on two machines, and why `toISOString()` always ends in `Z`: UTC is the only zone the value actually knows.

So you cannot put "3pm in Tokyo" into a `Date`. You can only store the instant that happened to be 3pm in Tokyo, and the label is gone. Carrying an instant and a zone together is what `Temporal.ZonedDateTime` is for.

options.text: Almost nothing. Many zones sit at UTC-4 in July, and the offset carries no rules
It is US Eastern Time, since `-04:00` in July means EDT
It is a zone that observes DST, since `-04:00` is a summer offset
It is `America/New_York` or `America/Toronto`, which are the only UTC-4 zones

questions.explanation:
On that instant, UTC-4 covers `America/New_York` (on DST), `America/Halifax` (on standard time), `America/Santo_Domingo` (which has no DST at all), `America/Manaus`, and `America/Puerto_Rico`, among others. An offset is the answer a zone gives for one moment. The zone is the whole rulebook.

Which matters because of the question you will eventually need to ask: what will this person's clock read three months from now? Only an IANA identifier can answer that, since only it carries the transitions and their history.

So offsets are fine for recording when something happened. Once you need to predict a clock reading, store `America/New_York` instead. "We store UTC everywhere" throws away the second capability without telling you.

questions.explanation:
The signs are inverted. `Etc/GMT+5` sits five hours behind UTC, because these zones follow the POSIX `TZ` convention where positive numbers count westward. That is the opposite of ISO 8601 and of how anyone speaks.

node -e 'console.log(new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en",{timeZone:"Etc/GMT+5",timeStyle:"long",hour12:false}).format(new Date("2026-01-15T12:00:00Z")))'

options.text: `EST` is permanently UTC-5 and never observes DST
They are aliases; `EST` is the short form of `America/New_York`

`EST` resolves, and it resolves to a fixed UTC-5 with no transitions:

```bash
node -e 'const f=z=>new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en",{timeZone:z,timeStyle:"long",hour12:false});
const t=new Date("2026-07-15T12:00:00Z");
console.log(f("EST").format(t), f("America/New_York").format(t))'
# 07:00:00 EST   08:00:00 EDT
```

The tz database keeps `Zone EST -5:00 - EST` in `backzone` purely for compatibility, and ICU takes a further step: ask it what `EST` canonicalizes to and it answers `America/Panama`, a zone that happens to be fixed at UTC-5. questions.title: How many instants correspond to `2026-03-08T02:30:00` in `America/New_York`?
questions.description: US DST begins on the second Sunday in March, which in 2026 is March 8.

images.alt: New York in 2026, drawn twice on a local wall clock. On 8 March the 02:00 cell is greyed out and marked “never happens”, so 2026-03-08T02:30 matches zero instants; Temporal's disambiguation options are listed — compatible pushes forward to 03:30 EDT, earlier and later pick the instants either side, reject throws — and the day has hoursInDay 23. On 1 November the 01:00 cell appears twice, so 01:15 EDT is 05:15Z while 01:45 EST is 06:45Z, making two log lines thirty clock-minutes apart ninety minutes apart in fact; an RFC 9557 stamp carrying both an offset and a zone name resolves which 01:30 was meant, and the day has hoursInDay 25. A closing table shows midnight plus 86,400,000 ms landing on 01:00 the next day, 09:00 on 7 March to 09:00 on 8 March being 23 hours, a 22:00-to-06:00 night shift on 31 October lasting 9 hours, and why startOfDay() exists.
images.caption: One hour missing, one hour twice — and every duration crossing them stops matching the clock.

options.text: Zero. That local time never occurs
One, the same as any other local time
Two, one in EST and one in EDT
One, but only if the year is not a leap year

questions.explanation:
At 02:00:00 EST the clocks jump to 03:00:00 EDT. The whole wall-clock hour from 02:00 up to 03:00 is missing from that date, so nothing at all maps to 02:30.

```bash
node -e 'const f=d=>new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US",{timeZone:"America/New_York",dateStyle:"short",timeStyle:"long",hour12:false}).format(d);
console.log(f(new Date("2026-03-08T06:59:00Z")), "->", f(new Date("2026-03-08T07:00:00Z")))'
# 3/8/26, 01:59:00 EST -> 3/8/26, 03:00:00 EDT
```

Going from a local time to an instant is thus a partial function. Feed a naive parser a value in the gap and it will throw, shift silently, or make something up, and the people who scheduled a 02:30 daily job are the ones who find out. Every serious date library makes you choose a policy for this rather than guessing on your behalf.

options.text: It throws, because the local time does not exist

questions.explanation:
The default is `disambiguation: "compatible"`, picked to match what `java.time` and other mature libraries already did. In a gap it acts like `"later"` and pushes the time forward by the size of the gap, so you land on 03:30. In the repeated hour after a fall-back it acts like `"earlier"` instead.

Your other choices are `"earlier"`, `"later"`, and `"reject"`, and choosing on purpose is the whole exercise. A scheduler usually wants `"later"` so the alarm still fires. An importer reconciling someone else's data usually wants `"reject"`, because a guess there is indistinguishable from a fact.

questions.explanation:
`reject`. Of the four values, `"compatible"` (the default), `"earlier"`, `"later"`, and `"reject"`, only the last raises a `RangeError` instead of choosing an instant for you.

The logger writes UTC but labels it as local, so the gap is a rendering artifact
A leap second was inserted between them, stretching the interval
It cannot happen; wall-clock ordering always matches instant ordering

questions.explanation:
At 02:00 EDT the clocks fall back to 01:00 EST, so everything from 01:00 to 01:59 happens twice, once at UTC-4 and again at UTC-5.

```bash
node -e 'const f=d=>new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US",{timeZone:"America/New_York",dateStyle:"short",timeStyle:"long",hour12:false}).format(d);
console.log(f(new Date("2026-11-01T05:30:00Z")), "|", f(new Date("2026-11-01T06:30:00Z")))'
# 11/1/26, 01:30:00 EDT | 11/1/26, 01:30:00 EST
```

01:15 EDT is 05:15Z and 01:45 EST is 06:45Z, ninety minutes apart. The nastier version of this is ordering: 01:45 EDT (05:45Z) sorts after 01:15 EST (06:15Z) but happened before it, so sorting by the local string can reverse cause and effect.

Log in UTC, or in a format that keeps the offset attached. A bare local wall time is not a total order.

options.text: The offset pins which of the two repeated 01:30s is meant; the zone name preserves the rules
The offset is redundant and exists only for parsers that cannot read the bracket suffix
The bracket suffix is a comment that parsers must ignore

questions.explanation:
This format is RFC 9557, the standard behind `Temporal.ZonedDateTime`'s string form, and each half does a job the other cannot.

The offset fixes the instant. On 2026-11-01 the local time 01:30 happens twice in New York, and `-04:00` says which one. The zone name keeps the rules around, so that later arithmetic ("plus one day", "same time next week") lands on the intended wall clock.

Drop the zone and calendar math becomes impossible. Drop the offset and one hour a year is unrecoverable. When the two contradict each other, which happens if tzdata changed after the value was written, Temporal's `offset` option decides the winner and defaults to refusing the value outright.

node -e 'const f=d=>new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US",{timeZone:"America/New_York",dateStyle:"short",timeStyle:"long",hour12:false}).format(d);

"Plus one day" and "plus 24 hours" are simply different operations. A one-off dentist appointment eighteen months from now
A store's "opens at 08:00" schedule
The moment a payment was authorized
An audit log entry for a failed login

questions.explanation:
One question sorts these: would the value change if a government changed the rules?

The past is settled. A payment or a log line happened at exactly one instant, so store UTC and render it in whatever zone the reader happens to want.

The future is a promise about a clock. The standup means "whenever Berliners call it 09:00", and the shop still opens at 08:00 if the EU abolishes DST next year. Store `09:00` alongside `Europe/Berlin` and work out the instant when you need it.

Flatten a future commitment into UTC and you have baked today's tzdata into your rows. When the rules move, and they move several times a year, those rows are quietly wrong and there is nothing left to recompute them from.

questions.title: A 2023 meeting stored as a UTC instant fired an hour late for Mexican attendees. Why?

images.alt: Three stacked layers. An instant is milliseconds since the epoch — one absolute point, with no zone and no calendar. An offset such as −04:00 is a number that was true at one instant and names no rules, since dozens of places share it every July. An IANA zone such as America/New_York is a rulebook saying which offset applies when, past and future, rewritten whenever a government changes the law. Beside them, what to store: a log line or past event as a UTC instant; a meeting at 09:00 next year as wall time plus an IANA zone, because the rules may change first; a date of birth as a plain calendar date; a weekly recurring event as wall time plus a zone, which is what iCalendar does. A closing list covers a JS Date holding one number and no zone, EST being a fixed −05:00 while the zone switches, Etc/GMT+5 actually meaning UTC−05:00, an offset never naming a zone, and a 2023 meeting stored as a UTC instant firing an hour late once Mexico dropped DST.

options.text: Mexico abolished DST for most of the country in late 2022, so the offset assumed at write time no longer applied
Mexico moved its whole territory one zone west, changing standard time
A leap second was inserted between the write and the meeting
UTC instants cannot be off by an hour; the client's clock had drifted

questions.explanation:
In October 2022 Mexico ended DST across most of the country, keeping it only in a strip along the US border. A 2023 appointment written before that law and converted to UTC under the old rules encoded an offset that had stopped existing, and drifted by exactly an hour.

None of this is unusual. Iran abolished DST in 2022, Egypt brought it back in 2023, Lebanon postponed its 2023 change with roughly two days' notice, and Morocco moves its transitions every year to follow Ramadan.

Converting more carefully does not help, because the information you need was thrown away at write time. Keep the wall time and the zone, and a routine tzdata update repairs your data for free.

options.text: It has no instant attached, so any zone conversion can shift it to the wrong calendar day
Timestamps cannot represent dates before 1970
Timestamp columns lose precision for values more than fifty years old
Timestamps store no year, only an offset from the current year

questions.explanation:
Nobody was born at `1990-05-14T00:00:00Z`. They were born on May 14, and it stays May 14 everywhere on Earth. A birthday is a calendar fact with no moment attached.

Put it in a timestamp and you have invented a midnight that never happened. One conversion later, from a client rendering in `America/Los_Angeles`, a JSON round-trip, or a report run in another region, the row says May 13. Age checks then flip on the wrong day, and nothing looks broken until somebody near a boundary complains.

Use a type that matches the concept: a Postgres `date`, `java.time.LocalDate`, `Temporal.PlainDate`. A value with no zone in it cannot be moved by one.

options.text: `Temporal.PlainMonthDay`
`Temporal.PlainDate` with the year set to 1970 by convention
`Temporal.PlainYearMonth`
`Temporal.Duration` measured from January 1

questions.explanation:
`Temporal.PlainMonthDay` is a month and a day with no year, which is exactly what "whose birthday is today" needs. No sentinel year, no special case for February 29. Its mirror image, `Temporal.PlainYearMonth`, covers a billing month such as `2026-03` with no particular day in it.

The pattern runs through the whole API: the type says what you know. `Instant` is an exact time with no calendar. `PlainDate` is a calendar date with no time or zone. `PlainDateTime` is a wall clock reading, which is why it cannot name an instant on its own. `ZonedDateTime` has all three. Reaching for the narrowest type turns the conversions that make no sense into code that will not compile, rather than code that runs and is wrong.

questions.title: Why does Temporal provide `startOfDay()` instead of letting you set the time to 00:00?

images.alt: New York in 2026, drawn twice on a local wall clock. On 8 March the 02:00 cell is greyed out and marked “never happens”, so 2026-03-08T02:30 matches zero instants; Temporal's disambiguation options are listed — compatible pushes forward to 03:30 EDT, earlier and later pick the instants either side, reject throws — and the day has hoursInDay 23. On 1 November the 01:00 cell appears twice, so 01:15 EDT is 05:15Z while 01:45 EST is 06:45Z, making two log lines thirty clock-minutes apart ninety minutes apart in fact; an RFC 9557 stamp carrying both an offset and a zone name resolves which 01:30 was meant, and the day has hoursInDay 25. A closing table shows midnight plus 86,400,000 ms landing on 01:00 the next day, 09:00 on 7 March to 09:00 on 8 March being 23 hours, a 22:00-to-06:00 night shift on 31 October lasting 9 hours, and why startOfDay() exists.
images.caption: One hour missing, one hour twice — and every duration crossing them stops matching the clock.

options.text: In some zones a DST transition happens at midnight, so 00:00 does not exist on that date
It is a convenience alias that always returns 00:00, just more readable
It rounds to the nearest hour to avoid sub-second precision loss
It returns 00:00 UTC rather than 00:00 local, which is what most callers want

questions.explanation:
A few zones move their clocks at midnight, which deletes the beginning of the day. Cuba starts DST at 00:00 local, so in Havana the earliest local time that exists on 2026-03-08 is 01:00:

```bash
node -e 'const f=d=>new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en",{timeZone:"America/Havana",dateStyle:"short",timeStyle:"long",hour12:false}).format(d);
console.log(f(new Date("2026-03-08T04:30:00Z")),"->",f(new Date("2026-03-08T05:30:00Z")))'
# 3/7/26, 23:30:00 GMT-5 -> 3/8/26, 01:30:00 GMT-4
```

Chile does the same thing. `startOfDay()` therefore returns the first instant that genuinely exists on that date in that zone, which is what a "today" query boundary actually needs. Hardcode `T00:00:00` and on those dates you have handed your library a time that never happened.

options.text: `24`, since a day is 24 hours by definition
`23.5`, because the transition is measured from the previous midnight

questions.explanation:
`23`. Temporal puts `hoursInDay` on `ZonedDateTime` because "a day is 24 hours" is false about twice a year in most inhabited zones. March 8, 2026 loses an hour in New York, and November 1 gains one and reports `25`.

It is not even always a whole number. Lord Howe Island shifts by half an hour, so its transition days run 23.5 and 24.5 hours.

Progress bars, billing periods, and any "percent of the day elapsed" figure computed by dividing by 24 will be wrong on those dates. Ask the calendar what the day was worth.

questions.title: By how many minutes does Lord Howe Island shift its clocks for daylight saving?
questions.description: Answer with the number of minutes.
questions.explanation:
`30`. `Australia/Lord_Howe` runs at UTC+10:30 on standard time and UTC+11:00 on daylight time, the only half-hour DST shift in the tz database.

```bash
node -e 'const f=d=>new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en",{timeZone:"Australia/Lord_Howe",timeStyle:"long"}).format(d);
console.log(f(new Date("2026-01-15T12:00:00Z")), f(new Date("2026-07-15T12:00:00Z")))'
# 11:00:00 PM GMT+11   10:30:00 PM GMT+10:30
```

So much for `dstOffset === 3600`. The base offsets are not whole hours either: `Pacific/Chatham` sits at UTC+12:45 and UTC+13:45, `Australia/Eucla` at UTC+08:45, `Asia/Kathmandu` at UTC+05:45. Store offsets in minutes or seconds, never in hours.

questions.title: How many minutes ahead of UTC is `Asia/Kathmandu`?
questions.description: Answer with the total number of minutes.
questions.explanation:
`345`. Nepal is at UTC+05:45, so five hours of 60 minutes plus 45.

```bash
node -e 'console.log(new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en",{timeZone:"Asia/Kathmandu",timeStyle:"long"}).format(new Date("2026-01-15T12:00:00Z")))'
# 5:45:00 PM GMT+5:45
```

Nepal chose to sit fifteen minutes ahead of India, which is itself at UTC+05:30. A zone picker built out of whole hours, or a schema with an `offset_hours INT` column, cannot represent Nepal, India, the Marquesas at UTC-09:30, or Chatham at UTC+12:45.

questions.title: How many different calendar dates can be in use around the world at the same moment?
questions.description: Count only zones that are actually inhabited and in regular use.

options.text: Three, for about one hour each day
Two, always
Two normally, and three only when DST is active somewhere
Four, once the International Date Line is crossed

questions.explanation:
Inhabited offsets span 25 hours, from `Pacific/Kiritimati` at UTC+14 down to `Pacific/Niue` and `Pacific/Pago_Pago` at UTC-11. Anything wider than 24 hours means two dates are not enough to describe the world:

```bash
node -e 'const at="2026-06-15T10:30:00Z", f=z=>new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en",{timeZone:z,dateStyle:"short"}).format(new Date(at));
console.log(f("Pacific/Kiritimati"), f("UTC"), f("Pacific/Niue"))'
# 6/16/26 6/15/26 6/14/26
```

Three dates at once, every day, for the hour between 10:00Z and 11:00Z. Counting the uninhabited UTC-12 islands stretches the span to 26 hours.

Which means "what day is it" has no server-side answer. A query like `WHERE created_at::date = CURRENT_DATE` quietly means "the date where the database happens to be", and that is nobody's date in particular.

questions.title: How many hours ahead of UTC is the furthest-forward time zone in regular use?
questions.description: Answer with the number of hours.
questions.explanation:
`14`. `Pacific/Kiritimati`, in Kiribati's Line Islands, has been UTC+14 since 1995, when the country moved its eastern islands across the date line so that the whole of Kiribati shared one calendar day.

That is why validating offsets against a `-12:00` to `+12:00` range is wrong, and why "two places can't be more than a day apart" fails. Add the UTC-12 islands at the other end and the span reaches 26 hours, so New Year's Day exists somewhere on Earth for a full 50 hours.

RFC 3339 allows offsets all the way to plus or minus 23:59, so the format never has to guess where politics will stop.

questions.title: Which ISO 8601 week date does the calendar date 2025-12-29 have?

options.text: `2026-W00-1`, since the year has not started yet

questions.explanation:
ISO weeks start on Monday, and week 1 is the one containing the year's first Thursday. January 1, 2026 is a Thursday, so week 1 of 2026 runs from Monday December 29, 2025 to Sunday January 4, 2026. December 29 is the first day of that week.

```bash
node -e 'console.log(new Date(Date.UTC(2026,0,1)).getUTCDay(), new Date(Date.UTC(2025,11,29)).getUTCDay())'
# 4 1   (Thursday, Monday)
```

The week-numbering year is a separate field from the calendar year, and the two disagree for a few days in most years. Group weekly metrics by `YEAR(date)` and `WEEK(date)` and you split one week across two buckets. There is also no `W00`, and some years run to `W53`.

questions.title: What is the difference between the ISO 8601 durations `P1M` and `PT1M`?

options.text: `P1M` is one month; `PT1M` is one minute
`P1M` is one minute; `PT1M` is one month
They are equivalent; `T` only marks the start of the time part for readability
`P1M` is one month; `PT1M` is invalid because minutes need `Min`

questions.explanation:
`M` means months before the `T` and minutes after it. That single letter is doing all the work, and dropping it turns a one-minute retry delay into a one-month one.

ISO 8601 hands `Y M D` to the date part and `H M S` to the time part, and leans entirely on `T` to sort out the shared `M`. No other letter collides.

There is a subtler issue underneath. `P1M` has no fixed length, since a month is anywhere from 28 to 31 days, and even `P1D` is 23, 24, or 25 hours depending on the zone and date. Only the components after `T` are exact, which is why Temporal will not convert between calendar units and exact units unless you give it a reference point to measure from.

questions.title: Which timestamps are valid ISO 8601 but rejected by RFC 3339?
questions.explanation:
RFC 3339 is a narrow profile of ISO 8601 rather than another name for it. Its grammar accepts only the extended calendar-date form with a mandatory offset, which rules out three things here:

- `24:00`, the ISO spelling for the midnight that ends a date. RFC 3339's `time-hour` runs from `00` to `23`.
- Basic format with the separators stripped out.
- Week dates, and ordinal dates like `2026-032`. Incidentally `2026-W03-4` is Thursday January 15, 2026, the same day as the other examples.

What it does accept is any number of fractional-second digits and any offset within plus or minus 23:59.

So "we accept ISO 8601" promises far more than most parsers deliver. If your API claims ISO 8601 and your parser is `Date.parse`, then `-00:00`, week dates, and durations are all going to surprise somebody. Say RFC 3339 and mean it.

questions.title: In RFC 3339, how does the offset `-00:00` differ from `+00:00`?

options.text: `+00:00` asserts UTC, while `-00:00` means the local offset is unknown
They are identical; the sign on zero is not significant
`-00:00` means UTC and `+00:00` means an unspecified zone
`-00:00` is invalid and must be written as `Z`

questions.explanation:
RFC 3339 gives `-00:00` its own meaning: the instant is known, but the offset the sender's own clock was using is not. Both `Z` and `+00:00` assert UTC positively.

It is an unusual piece of semantics to hang on a minus sign, and nearly every parser flattens it to zero on the way in, so the distinction disappears without anyone noticing. If you genuinely need to record "instant known, zone unknown", put it in a field of its own instead of trusting a convention your libraries will discard.

questions.title: When is sorting ISO 8601 timestamp strings lexicographically the same as sorting by instant?

options.text: Only when every value uses the same offset, the same field widths, and the same fractional precision
Always. Chronological ordering is the point of ISO 8601
Whenever every value carries an explicit offset, whatever that offset is
Only for dates after 1970, since earlier years sort as negative numbers

questions.explanation:
The big-endian field order does make byte order match time order, but only inside one fixed shape. Mix shapes and it falls apart.

Mixed offsets are the obvious case. `2026-01-15T09:00:00+05:30` sorts *after* `2026-01-15T08:00:00Z` because `09` beats `08` as text, yet it happens four and a half hours earlier.

Mixed precision is the sneaky one, because the culprit is the character before the digits:

```bash
node -e 'const a="2026-01-15T12:00:00Z", b="2026-01-15T12:00:00.500Z";
console.log(a<b ? "a sorts first" : "b sorts first", "| b is", Date.parse(b)-Date.parse(a), "ms later")'
# b sorts first | b is 500 ms later
```

`.` is byte 0x2E and `Z` is 0x5A, so a value carrying a fractional part sorts before the same second without one, while actually happening later. Expanded years such as `+012026` break the field widths outright.

Normalize to UTC with a fixed number of fractional digits before letting a string comparator near a timeline. Sorting the epoch integer instead sidesteps the whole question.

questions.title: How does POSIX "seconds since the Epoch" handle a leap second?

options.text: It cannot represent one. The formula assumes every day has exactly 86400 seconds
It inserts value 61 in the seconds field, matching UTC's 23:59:60
It adds one to the epoch count, so Unix time runs 27 seconds behind UTC
It pauses the counter for one second, so two instants share a value

questions.explanation:
POSIX defines the count with an arithmetic formula over the broken-down date, roughly `tm_sec + tm_min*60 + tm_hour*3600 + tm_yday*86400` plus year terms, and there is no leap-second term anywhere in it. Every day is 86400 seconds by construction, so `23:59:60` has nowhere to go.

What a system does with the real leap second is left to the implementation, which is the actual problem. Some repeat a value. Google-style leap smearing spreads the extra second over several hours so that NTP clients never see a repeat at all.

Either way the count is not the true number of elapsed SI seconds since 1970. It is 27 short, and it makes a poor stopwatch for anything that cares about physics.

questions.title: By how many seconds does TAI lead UTC as of 2026?
questions.description: Answer with the number of seconds.
questions.explanation:
`37`. UTC took its modern form in 1972 already 10 seconds behind TAI, and 27 leap seconds have been added since, the last of them at the end of December 31, 2016. The difference has been 37 seconds since January 1, 2017.

Every leap second so far has been positive. A negative one, which would skip 23:59:59, has never happened, though it is now the more likely direction because Earth's rotation has recently sped up.

UTC is therefore not a uniform timescale, and any code assuming 86400 seconds per day is assuming something UTC never offered. TAI and GPS time are uniform; UTC gives that up in exchange for staying within 0.9 seconds of solar time.

questions.title: What did the 2022 General Conference on Weights and Measures decide about leap seconds?

options.text: To stop inserting them, by widening the allowed gap between UTC and UT1 no later than 2035
To insert them on a fixed schedule every four years, like leap days
To replace UTC with TAI as the world's civil timescale in 2035
To move responsibility for announcing them from the IERS to the ITU

questions.explanation:
Resolution 4 of the 27th CGPM, in November 2022, resolved to increase the tolerated difference between UTC and UT1 by 2035 at the latest, which in practice ends leap-second insertion. That tolerance had been 0.9 seconds since 1972.

The reasoning was operational rather than scientific. Leap seconds have broken production systems repeatedly, and a negative leap second, which has never been attempted, looked considerably riskier than letting civil time drift slowly away from solar time.

Nothing about the past changes. The historical leap seconds stay in the record, TAI stays 37 seconds ahead of UTC, and Unix time still does not count real elapsed seconds across the years from 1972 to 2016.

questions.title: Why should elapsed-time measurements not use the wall clock?

options.text: The wall clock can be stepped backwards by NTP or an operator, producing negative durations
The wall clock has only second resolution on most platforms
The wall clock stops while the process is descheduled
The wall clock is stored as a 32-bit value and overflows during long measurements

questions.explanation:
`CLOCK_REALTIME` and `Date.now()` follow civil time, and civil time is adjustable. NTP can slew or step it, an administrator can set it by hand, and a suspended VM can resume with a corrected clock. Subtract two readings across any of that and your elapsed value comes out negative or absurdly large, which shows up as a timeout that fires instantly or never fires at all.

Use a clock that promises only one thing, that it never runs backwards: `CLOCK_MONOTONIC`, `performance.now()`, `System.nanoTime()`, Rust's `Instant`. None of them has a meaningful epoch and none can be formatted as a date, which is the point.

When did this happen and how long did this take are separate questions, and they want separate clocks.

One: UTC-6, US Central Standard Time
Two: UTC-6 in winter and UTC-5 in summer
One. Abbreviations are registered with IANA and are unique

questions.title: What does PostgreSQL physically store in a `timestamptz` column?

options.text: A UTC instant only. The input's offset is used to convert, then discarded
The local time plus the offset it was supplied with
The local time plus the IANA zone name from the session's `TimeZone` setting
The literal text as supplied, parsed only on retrieval

questions.explanation:
The name lies a little: `timestamp with time zone` stores no time zone. It is an eight-byte microsecond count measured from 2000-01-01 UTC. On the way in, the offset you supplied (or the session `TimeZone` if you supplied none) converts the literal to UTC and is then discarded. On the way out, the value is rendered in the session's `TimeZone`.

Two clients inserting the same instant from Tokyo and Berlin therefore produce byte-identical rows, and one row displays differently to two sessions. For recording when something happened, that is exactly right.

What you cannot get back is which zone the user meant. When that matters, for a future appointment or a shop's opening hour, add a `text` column holding the IANA identifier next to it. A `timestamptz` on its own answers only half the question.

questions.title: What type and value does `timestamptz '2026-01-15 12:00:00+00' AT TIME ZONE 'America/New_York'` produce?

options.text: `timestamp without time zone`, `2026-01-15 07:00:00`
`timestamp with time zone`, `2026-01-15 12:00:00+00`
`timestamp with time zone`, `2026-01-15 17:00:00+00`
`timestamp without time zone`, `2026-01-15 12:00:00`

questions.explanation:
`AT TIME ZONE` converts between the two timestamp types, and which direction it goes depends on what you hand it:

```sql
-- timestamptz -> timestamp: "render this instant as a wall clock there"
SELECT timestamptz '2026-01-15 12:00:00+00' AT TIME ZONE 'America/New_York';
-- 2026-01-15 07:00:00

-- timestamp -> timestamptz: "this wall clock was there; give me the instant"
SELECT timestamp '2026-01-15 12:00:00' AT TIME ZONE 'America/New_York';
-- 2026-01-15 17:00:00+00
```

One operator, two opposite meanings. Read it as "convert to this zone" and you will get one of the two cases backwards every time, and what comes back is a plausible-looking timestamp rather than an error.

The way to remember it: the clause supplies whichever zone the value was missing, and hands you the other type.

questions.title: Why is `BETWEEN '2026-01-15 00:00' AND '2026-01-15 23:59:59.999'` the wrong way to select one day?

options.text: It silently drops the final sub-millisecond slice; a half-open `>= day AND < next day` cannot
`BETWEEN` is exclusive at both ends, so it also drops midnight
`BETWEEN` cannot be used with timestamp types at all
It works correctly but prevents the planner from using an index

questions.explanation:
`BETWEEN` includes both ends, which forces you to name the last representable instant of the day, and you will get its precision wrong. PostgreSQL timestamps hold microseconds, so `23:59:59.999` quietly excludes everything from `23:59:59.999001` onwards. On a nanosecond store the hole is a thousand times wider.

A half-open range has no such edge to get wrong:

```sql
WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-15' AND created_at < '2026-01-16'
```

It does not care about the column's precision, it tiles consecutive days with no gaps or overlaps, and an index can still serve it.

One more thing for a `timestamptz` column: those boundaries are instants, so compute them with `AT TIME ZONE` for the zone the user means. January 15 starts at a different instant in Auckland than in Los Angeles.

questions.title: How does MySQL's `TIMESTAMP` type differ from `DATETIME` in its handling of zones?

options.text: `TIMESTAMP` converts from the session zone to UTC on write and back on read; `DATETIME` stores the literal unchanged
`DATETIME` converts to UTC on write; `TIMESTAMP` stores the literal unchanged
Both convert to UTC, but `DATETIME` also stores the original offset
Neither converts; `TIMESTAMP` merely has a narrower supported range

questions.explanation:
`TIMESTAMP` is zone-aware across the round trip. MySQL converts the value from the session's `time_zone` to UTC when writing and converts it back when reading. `DATETIME` is inert, and the characters you put in are the characters you get out regardless of session zone.

The trap is that a `TIMESTAMP` column's displayed value depends on who is reading it, so the same untouched rows produce different times in a report run under a different `time_zone`. `TIMESTAMP` also only spans 1970 to 2038, which you will discover from a range error at an inconvenient moment.

The choice comes down to the same split as everywhere else: `TIMESTAMP` for when something happened, `DATETIME` for what the clock said, plus a column naming the zone if you will need to resolve it later.

questions.title: An API sends `"createdAt": 1767225600` and the UI renders January 1970. What went wrong?

options.text: The value is epoch seconds but the `Date` constructor takes milliseconds
The value overflowed 32 bits and wrapped to near the epoch
The value is negative, and `Date` clamps negatives to 1970
`Date` needs a string; passing a number always yields the epoch

questions.explanation:
`1767225600` is seconds, Unix time for `2026-01-01T00:00:00Z`. Read as milliseconds it comes to about 20.5 days, which lands in January 1970.

```bash
node -e 'console.log(new Date(1767225600).toISOString(), new Date(1767225600*1000).toISOString())'
# 1970-01-21T10:53:45.600Z 2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z
```

Seconds are the POSIX and JWT convention, used by `exp`, `iat`, and `nbf`. Milliseconds are the JavaScript and Java convention. Both arrive as bare integers, so nothing objects, and the failure is a believable date in 1970. Multiply by a thousand twice and you land in the year 57971 instead.

Guard it at the boundary. Name the field for its unit, as in `createdAtEpochSeconds`, or send an RFC 3339 string, which cannot be misread by a factor of a thousand.

questions.title: What is the largest value a signed 32-bit `time_t` can hold?
questions.description: Answer with the number of seconds.
questions.explanation:
`2147483647`, which is `2**31 - 1`, or `2038-01-19T03:14:07Z`. A second later the value wraps to -2147483648 and the clock reads December 1901.

```bash
node -e 'console.log(new Date(2147483647000).toISOString())'
# 2038-01-19T03:14:07.000Z
```

Most 64-bit systems widened `time_t` years ago, but the value still leaks through fixed-width wire formats, MySQL `TIMESTAMP` columns, embedded firmware, and any schema keeping epoch seconds in an `INT`. Thirty-year mortgages and long-dated bonds already cross it.

JavaScript's own ceiling is elsewhere. `Date` tops out at plus or minus 8.64e15 milliseconds, roughly 273,790 years either side of the epoch, and anything past that is an invalid date.

questions.title: What does `JSON.stringify({ at: new Date(NaN) })` produce?

options.text: `{"at":null}`
It throws a `RangeError` for an invalid time value
`{"at":"Invalid Date"}`
`{"at":NaN}`

questions.explanation:
`Date.prototype.toJSON` checks whether the value is finite and returns `null` when it is not, so an invalid date serializes quietly instead of throwing.

```bash
node -e 'console.log(JSON.stringify({at:new Date(NaN)})); try{new Date(NaN).toISOString()}catch(e){console.log(e.name)}'
# {"at":null}
# RangeError
```

Call `toISOString()` yourself and the same value does throw, so one bad date is loud on one path and silent on the other. Through the serializer it becomes a `null` column with no stack trace pointing anywhere useful.

Check it where you parse, with `Number.isNaN(d.getTime())`, or use a parser that rejects bad input rather than handing back a sentinel.

questions.title: Does `2026-01-30` plus one month plus one day equal the same date as plus one day plus one month?
questions.description: Assume the default `overflow: "constrain"` behaviour, which clamps an invalid day to the end of the month. February 2026 has 28 days.

options.text: No. One order gives 2026-03-01 and the other gives 2026-02-28
Yes, both give 2026-03-01
Yes, both give 2026-02-28
No, but only in leap years, where February has 29 days

questions.explanation:
Take the month first: January 30 plus a month wants February 30, which does not exist, so it clamps to February 28. Add a day and you get March 1.

Take the day first: January 30 plus a day is January 31. Add a month, which wants February 31, and it clamps to February 28.

March 1 against February 28, from the same two additions. Calendar arithmetic is neither commutative nor associative, because clamping throws away the information you would need to undo it, and `constrain`, `reject`, and rolling over to March 2 are all defensible policies, so libraries disagree.

Two things follow. Adding a month has no inverse, since January 31 goes to February 28 and comes back as January 28. And monthly billing needs an explicit anchor day rather than repeated addition. Temporal's answer is to add larger units before smaller ones within a single `add()` call, and to let you pick the `overflow` behaviour.

questions.title: Why does the tz database model `Europe/Dublin` as having negative daylight saving in winter?

options.text: Irish law defines UTC+1 as standard time, so winter is a departure from it rather than the baseline
It is a long-standing bug in the tzdb, kept for backward compatibility
Ireland observes DST year-round on a two-step schedule
The rules track the UK's, and Dublin is only a compatibility link to London

questions.explanation:
Irish statute names Irish Standard Time as the summer time at UTC+1 and treats the winter period as the deviation. Since tzdata 2018a the `europe` source models that literally, applying a negative saving in October rather than a positive one in March:

```text
Rule	Eire	1981	max	-	Mar	lastSun	 1:00u	0	-
Rule	Eire	1996	max	-	Oct	lastSun	 1:00u	-1:00	-
```

The clock readings come out identical to `Europe/London`. Only the bookkeeping differs, and that bookkeeping does not travel well: whether a platform actually reports `tm_isdst = 1` in January depends on how its `TZif` files were compiled and which library reads them, so two machines can disagree about whether Dublin is "on DST" right now.

Treat `isDST` accordingly. It tells you which of a zone's rule sets is active, its sign is an artifact of legal drafting, and it should not be driving application logic. To ask whether summer time is in effect, compare the current offset against the zone's own winter offset. To show a user something, ask the formatter for the zone name.

questions.title: What happened to Friday, 30 December 2011 in Samoa?

options.text: It never existed. Samoa jumped the date line, going from Thursday the 29th to Saturday the 31st
It occurred twice, as Samoa moved east across the date line
It was shortened to 23 hours by an unusually large DST transition
Nothing; the change took effect at the start of 2012 instead

questions.explanation:
Samoa moved from UTC-11 to UTC+13 so that its working week lined up with Australia and New Zealand instead of trailing them by a day. Clocks went from 23:59:59 on Thursday December 29 straight to 00:00:00 on Saturday December 31. The 30th did not happen, and nor did anybody's birthday.

The tz database records it as a single offset change of a full day:

```text
Zone Pacific/Apia	...
			-11:00	WS	%z	2011 Dec 29 24:00
			 13:00	WS	%z
```

So a zone's offset can move by 24 hours, and a calendar date can be missing from a zone's history altogether. That breaks any loop that steps day by day and formats each one, and any `daysBetween` computed from calendar arithmetic rather than from the zone's own rules.

Kiribati did much the same in 1995, and Kwajalein in 1993. Offsets are political.

questions.title: What offset does the tz database record for Brussels before standard time was adopted?

options.text: UTC+00:17:30, the city's local mean solar time
UTC+00:00, since standard offsets are defined back to 1847
UTC+01:00, extrapolating today's rules backwards
No offset at all; tzdata's history begins in 1970

questions.explanation:
The `europe` source file opens the zone on Brussels' local mean time:

```text
Zone Europe/Brussels	0:17:30 -	LMT	1880
```

Kolkata's is `5:53:28`, Kyiv's `2:02:04`, Berlin's `0:53:28`.

Historical offsets therefore need second precision, which an `offset_minutes` column cannot round-trip and `Date.prototype.getTimezoneOffset()` cannot represent at all, since it returns whole minutes. And tzdata only guarantees correctness from 1970 onwards; earlier values are best-effort.

That pre-1970 record is also shrinking. Zones whose clocks have agreed since 1970 get merged, so `Europe/Amsterdam` is now just a `Link` to `Europe/Brussels` in the `backward` file. It still resolves, but Amsterdam's own historical offset of `0:19:32` has moved out of the main data into `backzone`. Genealogy and legal history are poor fits for a general-purpose zone library.

questions.title: Why do Morocco's clock changes fall on different dates each year?

options.text: It leaves UTC+1 for UTC+0 during Ramadan, which moves earlier by about 11 days a year
It follows the EU schedule but with a one-week delay that shifts annually
Its transitions are tied to the equinoxes rather than to fixed dates
It sets them by decree each year with no underlying rule

questions.explanation:
`Africa/Casablanca` stays at UTC+1 year-round and drops to UTC+0 for Ramadan. The Islamic calendar is lunar, so Ramadan arrives roughly 11 days earlier in the Gregorian year each time, and the transition dates move with it. tzdata carries computed rules for years ahead.

Two assumptions die here at once: that transitions happen in spring and autumn, and that a zone has at most two of them on a stable schedule.

It is also why no zone's behaviour fits in a sentence like "UTC+1, DST from March to October". Ask the tz database about a specific instant, and never reimplement a country's rules in application code.

questions.title: How does iCalendar keep a weekly meeting on the same wall clock across a DST change?

images.alt: Three stacked layers. An instant is milliseconds since the epoch — one absolute point, with no zone and no calendar. An offset such as −04:00 is a number that was true at one instant and names no rules, since dozens of places share it every July. An IANA zone such as America/New_York is a rulebook saying which offset applies when, past and future, rewritten whenever a government changes the law. Beside them, what to store: a log line or past event as a UTC instant; a meeting at 09:00 next year as wall time plus an IANA zone, because the rules may change first; a date of birth as a plain calendar date; a weekly recurring event as wall time plus a zone, which is what iCalendar does. A closing list covers a JS Date holding one number and no zone, EST being a fixed −05:00 while the zone switches, Etc/GMT+5 actually meaning UTC−05:00, an offset never naming a zone, and a 2023 meeting stored as a UTC instant firing an hour late once Mexico dropped DST.
images.caption: The instant stayed correct; the intention — nine in the morning, where they live — did not.

options.text: `DTSTART` carries a `TZID`, and the `RRULE` is expanded in that zone's local time
`DTSTART` is stored in UTC and the `RRULE` adds a DST correction per occurrence
Each occurrence is materialized as its own UTC instant when the event is created
An `RDATE` override must be added manually for every transition

questions.explanation:
RFC 5545 keeps the rule in local terms and expands it in the named zone:

```text
DTSTART;TZID=America/New_York:20260302T090000
RRULE:FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=MO
```

Every occurrence is 09:00 in New York. The instants they resolve to sit 23 or 25 hours apart across a transition, which is the correct answer rather than a rounding error.

Store the same event as pre-expanded UTC instants and it drifts by an hour twice a year. Worse, it cannot be repaired when a government rewrites the rules, because the intent behind the instants is gone.

This works outside calendars too. Persist the rule, meaning local time plus zone plus recurrence, and derive instants when you read. Materialize them only as a cache you are willing to throw away and rebuild.

questions.title: How many hours does a New York night shift from 22:00 on 2026-10-31 to 06:00 on 2026-11-01 last?
questions.description: DST ends on November 1, 2026. Answer with the number of hours.

images.alt: New York in 2026, drawn twice on a local wall clock. On 8 March the 02:00 cell is greyed out and marked “never happens”, so 2026-03-08T02:30 matches zero instants; Temporal's disambiguation options are listed — compatible pushes forward to 03:30 EDT, earlier and later pick the instants either side, reject throws — and the day has hoursInDay 23. On 1 November the 01:00 cell appears twice, so 01:15 EDT is 05:15Z while 01:45 EST is 06:45Z, making two log lines thirty clock-minutes apart ninety minutes apart in fact; an RFC 9557 stamp carrying both an offset and a zone name resolves which 01:30 was meant, and the day has hoursInDay 25. A closing table shows midnight plus 86,400,000 ms landing on 01:00 the next day, 09:00 on 7 March to 09:00 on 8 March being 23 hours, a 22:00-to-06:00 night shift on 31 October lasting 9 hours, and why startOfDay() exists.
images.caption: One hour missing, one hour twice — and every duration crossing them stops matching the clock.

questions.explanation:
`9`. Clocking on at 22:00 EDT is 02:00Z, and clocking off at 06:00 EST is 11:00Z.

```bash
node -e 'console.log((Date.parse("2026-11-01T11:00:00Z")-Date.parse("2026-11-01T02:00:00Z"))/3600000)'
# 9
```

The wall clocks claim eight hours. The worker was there for nine and, in most jurisdictions, is owed nine. Run the same shift in March and it is seven.

Payroll, SLA timers, and any "time spent" figure therefore have to subtract instants rather than local clock readings. Convert to UTC or `Temporal.Instant` first, then take the difference. Users who see the duration printed next to two local times will think the arithmetic is broken, and it is worth explaining rather than hiding.

questions.title: How should a browser determine the user's IANA time zone?

options.text: `Intl.DateTimeFormat().resolvedOptions().timeZone`
Derive it from `new Date().getTimezoneOffset()`
Parse the abbreviation out of `new Date().toString()`
Look it up from the `Accept-Language` header's region subtag

questions.explanation:
`Intl.DateTimeFormat().resolvedOptions().timeZone` returns the host's IANA identifier, something like `"Europe/Berlin"`. It is the only one of these that produces a zone at all.

An offset is a single sample of a function, so UTC+1 in January cannot tell Berlin apart from Lagos, which never changes. The abbreviation in `toString()` is locale-dependent display text and ambiguous besides. And locale is not geography: `en-US` says nothing about which of the American zones, and plenty of people run a locale from a country they left years ago.

Read it on the client and send it, rather than guessing on the server. That call and `Temporal.Now.timeZoneId()` both report the operating system setting, which is the closest thing to the user's own answer.

questions.title: Why did calendar software show wrong times in March 2007 in the United States?

options.text: The Energy Policy Act of 2005 moved the DST start earlier, so systems with hardcoded pre-2007 rules were an hour off
A leap second was inserted in March 2007, shifting stored instants
The United States switched from UTC to TAI as its civil time basis
Several states adopted permanent DST, changing their standard offsets

questions.explanation:
From 2007, US DST began on the second Sunday in March and ended on the first Sunday in November, replacing a rule that had started it in April. Anything that had not taken a tzdata update, whether an embedded device, an unpatched server, or code with the rules written into it, was an hour wrong for the three weeks in between. People called it a mini-Y2K at the time.

Which is the case for treating zone rules as data you update rather than logic you compile. IANA publishes several releases a year, and a container image or a phone that stopped receiving updates will drift away from everyone else.

Worth checking what your own stack actually reads: the OS tzdata, a copy bundled with your language runtime, or a vendored library. A single process can be running more than one version of the answer.
